events.title: Spring Framework 1.0 released
events.summary: On March 24, 2004, Rod Johnson's team shipped Spring Framework 1.0 — a lighter way to build [Java] web and enterprise apps.
events.about: Spring replaced heavy application-server requirements with plain [Java] classes, automatic wiring of components, and modular configuration. It powers [REST] APIs, [microservices] (via [Spring Boot]), batch jobs, and banking backends. [Spring Boot] later made running a [Java] web service as simple as launching a single file.

narrative.whyChosen: Spring became the default [Java] enterprise stack and influenced how apps are structured across the industry.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved [Java] apps could be modular and testable without bulky enterprise server containers.
narrative.problemSolved: Enterprise [Java] development was verbose and tied to heavy servers; teams needed a simpler way to assemble and test applications.

events.title: RubyGems released
events.summary: Chad Fowler, Jim Weirich, and collaborators released RubyGems on March 14, 2004 — a standard package format and `gem` command for [Ruby] libraries.
events.about: RubyGems packages code as gems with versioned dependencies — `gem install rails` pulls transitive libraries from rubygems.org. It enabled the Rails ecosystem, Capistrano deploys, and thousands of reusable [Ruby] libraries. Bundler later layered lockfiles on top, but RubyGems remains the foundation every `Gemfile` resolves against.

narrative.whyChosen: RubyGems gave [Ruby] a standard package manager years before it shipped with the language.
narrative.whyImportant: It unlocked reusable library distribution and made Rails' gem-based ecosystem possible.
narrative.problemSolved: [Ruby] developers manually vendored libraries with no central registry or dependency resolution.

events.title: Atlassian Confluence 1.0 released
events.summary: Atlassian released Confluence 1.0 on March 25, 2004 — a team [wiki] for documentation, specs, and runbooks alongside [Jira] tickets.
events.about: Confluence became where engineering teams wrote RFCs, onboarding docs, and postmortems — linked from [Jira] issues and [Bitbucket] PRs. Its [WYSIWYG] editor and page permissions made internal wikis approachable before Notion; many enterprises still treat Confluence as the system of record for technical knowledge.

narrative.whyChosen: Confluence paired with [Jira] to own engineering documentation and ticketing.
narrative.whyImportant: It standardized internal wikis for specs, runbooks, and retrospectives.
narrative.problemSolved: [Teams] scattered docs across file shares and ad-hoc Word files with no search.
